label: Confabulation
summary: Confabulation is the tendency to produce plausible-sounding but invented information rather than acknowledging a gap. In Maaike's work it shows up as the core mechanism behind LLM hallucinations: the model fills in missing data confidently instead of stopping. It is not a fringe failure mode but a structural consequence of how LLMs approximate knowledge.
how_maaike_uses: Maaike uses confabulation both as a conceptual lens and as a lived problem. On the conceptual side she argues that hallucinations cannot be 'solved' without changing how LLMs fundamentally operate, because saying 'I don't know' requires an absolute TRUE/FALSE state the model can only approximate. On the practical side she documented a real incident where Claude confabulated a complete, structurally valid library entry, including a plausible author name drawn from her professional context, and published it on her site. That experience pushed her from theory into process design: she added a hard rule requiring Open Library verification before any book entry is written, treating empty fields as always safer than invented ones.
open_questions: Is there any architecture that would give an LLM a genuine 'I don't know' capability rather than a trained approximation of one?
The `ai: assisted` label flagged AI involvement but not AI invention — what label or safeguard would actually communicate the difference to readers?
A full audit of existing `ai: assisted` library entries is still pending, so the scope of prior confabulation in the garden is not yet known.
